Before we start — where we are

Phase 1 (Analysis) closed yesterday with Brick 4: Bricks 1 to 4 are your Project Proposal & Requirement Analysis. Today Phase 2 begins. From now on every Brick adds working code to JARVIS, and the code rests on one decision that we take today: which classes the program has, and what each one is responsible for.

The question of the hour is precise: which classes does JARVIS need, what does each one own, and how does the program read the studio's CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file into objects without crashing? We answer it in four short parts — one class written live, the loader, the class diagram, and the two abstract base classes — each followed by a four-minute activity.

5.1

Classes, objects and the dataclass: live coding TimeEntryClasses, objects & @dataclass

⏱ 0:00–0:11 · activity 0:11–0:15
▣ Slide 4 — 5.1 Classes, objects & @dataclass — key terms
Classes, objects and the dataclass: live coding TimeEntry
Objective of Lesson 5.1 · 0:00–0:11
Define a class with attributes and methods, create objects from it, and protect every object with validation at creation and immutability afterwards.

Key terms

Class
A named definition that groups data (attributes) and the operations on that data (methods). In Python a class is created by the class statement; TimeEntry is a class.
Object (instance)
One concrete value created from a class. It has its own attribute values and the methods of its class. first = TimeEntry(...) creates one object; type(first) is TimeEntry.
Attribute
A named value stored in an object (instance attribute, first.minutes) or in the class itself (class attribute).
Method
A function defined inside a class. Python passes the object on which it is called as the first parameter, named self by convention.
__init__
The special method that Python calls to initialise a new object right after it has been created; it receives the constructor arguments.
Special (dunder) method
A method whose name starts and ends with two underscores (__init__, __repr__, __str__, __eq__). Python calls it for a built-in operation such as creation, printing or ==.
Decorator
A callable applied with the @name syntax on the line above a function or class definition; it receives the definition and returns a modified version.
@dataclass
The decorator of the standard-library module dataclasses (Python 3.7, PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 557) that writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from the annotated fields of a class.
Field and type hint
In a dataclass, a class-level annotation such as minutes: int declares one field and its intended type. Python does not check the type when an object is created.
frozen=True
A dataclass option that makes every object read-only: assigning a field raises FrozenInstanceError. With eq=True (the default) it also generates __hash__.
__post_init__
A method that the generated __init__ calls after it has stored the fields; it is the place for validation.
Invariant
A condition that is true for every object of a class during its whole life, for example “minutes ≥ 0” for every TimeEntry.
Property
A method decorated with @property; it is read like an attribute (first.hours, without parentheses) and computed when read.
Encapsulation
Keeping data together with the code that uses it in one class, and controlling how that data can be read or changed from outside the class.
▣ Slide 5 — Why one row of the log needs a class

Why one row of the log needs a class

Our teaching dataset, boreal_routines_2026.csv, has 420 rows and nine columns. When Python reads one row with the csv module, it receives nine pieces of text: '2026-09-14', 'S1', 'email_triage', 'communication', '9', '36', '1', 'manual' and '1'. Text is a weak representation for a program. The minutes '36' cannot be added to other minutes, the date cannot be compared with another date, and nothing prevents a row with −19 minutes from entering the monthly cost report. In Bricks 3 and 4 your scripts worked on lists of dictionaries, which was acceptable for one script. JARVIS has two engines, a store, a reporter and several tools that all use the same rows, so the row is defined once, as a class, and every module uses that definition.

▣ Slide 6 — Class and object

Class and object

A class is a named definition that lists the data an object will hold (its attributes) and the operations it can perform (its methods). An object, also called an instance, is one concrete value built from that definition. TimeEntry is the class. S1's e-mail triage of Monday, September 14 (36 minutes, done by hand) is one object; S1's first assistant-triaged run of Friday, September 25 (19 minutes) is another object of the same class. Both objects have the same attribute names, each with its own values, and Python stores each object separately in memory.

Written without any help, the class starts like this:

class TimeEntryPlain:
    def __init__(self, date, staff_id, routine, minutes, tool):
        self.date = date
        self.staff_id = staff_id
        self.routine = routine
        self.minutes = minutes
        self.tool = tool
A hand-written class: one parameter and one assignment line per attribute (five of the nine columns shown).

__init__ is the method Python calls to initialise a new object; the expression TimeEntryPlain(date(2026, 9, 14), "S1", "email_triage", 36, "manual") creates the object and passes it to __init__ as self, followed by the five arguments. self.minutes = minutes stores the value of the parameter in an attribute of this particular object. With all nine columns, the class needs nine parameters and nine assignment lines, plus a __repr__ method for a readable display and an __eq__ method to compare two entries. The code is repetitive, and a typing error in one assignment line produces a bug that is difficult to see.

▣ Slide 7 — The @dataclass decorator
▣ Slide 8 — What @dataclass(frozen=True) writes for TimeEntry

The @dataclass decorator

A decorator is applied with the @ syntax on the line above a definition; it receives the class and returns a modified class. The decorator @dataclass, from the standard-library module dataclasses (added in Python 3.7 by PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 557), reads the annotated fields of the class and writes the repetitive methods for us:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TimeEntry:
    """One timed run of one routine by one staff member (one row of the time log)."""

    date: date
    staff_id: str
    routine: str
    category: str
    start_hour: int
    minutes: int
    interruptions: int
    tool: str
    done: bool
TimeEntry as a frozen dataclass: nine fields, one per column of boreal_routines_2026.csv.
Table 5.1.A — What @dataclass(frozen=True) generatesCSV
Method written by @dataclassWhat it does for TimeEntry
__init__Takes the nine fields as parameters, in the order of the class body, and stores them in the new object.
__repr__Returns TimeEntry(date=datetime.date(2026, 9, 14), staff_id='S1', …, done=True): the class name and every field.
__eq__Compares two entries field by field: two objects with the same nine values are equal.
__setattr__, __delattr__ (frozen)Raise FrozenInstanceError on any attempt to change or delete a field after creation.
__hash__ (frozen and eq)Computes a hash from the fields, so an entry can be stored in a set or used as a dictionary key.

Each line minutes: int is a type hint (an annotation). For a dataclass it has two roles: it declares the field, and it documents the type the field is meant to hold. Python itself does not check the type when the object is created: TimeEntry(..., interruptions="1", ...) is accepted by the generated __init__, and the text "1" stays in the object, because no check looks at that field. (A text in minutes would fail only by accident, when __post_init__ compares it with 0.) The loader of Lesson 5.2 therefore converts every text value to its type before it builds the object, and the class checks the values it must never accept.

▣ Slide 9 — Validation in __post_init__

Validation in __post_init__

The generated __init__ calls a method named __post_init__ right after it has stored the fields, if the class defines one. This is where TimeEntry checks its values. Three rules come from the data dictionary of Brick 2:

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if self.minutes < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"minutes must be >= 0, got {self.minutes}")
        if not 0 <= self.start_hour <= 23:
            raise ValueError(f"start_hour must be 0-23, got {self.start_hour}")
        if self.tool not in ALLOWED_TOOLS:          # {"manual", "template", "jarvis"}
            raise ValueError(f"unknown tool {self.tool!r}")
Three checks; each error message names the field and the value that failed.

If a check fails, raise ValueError(...) interrupts the creation: no object exists, and the caller receives the error with its message. S2's invoice check typed as −19 minutes produces minutes must be >= 0, got -19; the tool name jarvs produces unknown tool 'jarvs'. Combined with frozen=True, the checks establish an invariant: a condition that holds for every TimeEntry during its whole life. Every engine of JARVIS can rely on it — the statistics of Class 6 never meet a negative duration, because an object with a negative duration cannot be created and an object cannot be changed after creation.

▣ Slide 10 — Methods and properties

Methods and properties

A method is a function defined in the class body; it receives the object as self. The cost of one run uses only the data of that run, so it belongs to TimeEntry:

    def cost(self, hourly_value: float) -> float:
        return self.minutes / 60 * hourly_value
first.cost(28.0) returns 36 / 60 × 28 = 16.80 dollars.

The hourly value is a parameter, not a number written inside the method. The value of 28 $/h is one of the three given numbers of Class 3; it can change, and a team that writes 28 inside cost() hides an assumption in the code. A property is a method marked @property: it is read like an attribute, without parentheses, and computed at the moment it is read. first.hours returns 0.6. A property cannot disagree with the data it is computed from, which is the reason hours is a property and not a tenth field.

▣ Slide 11 — Encapsulation in Python

Encapsulation in Python

Encapsulation means that the data and the code that uses it live in the same class, and that the class controls how its data can be read or changed. Python has no private keyword; it uses two conventions described in the official tutorial (section Private Variables):

  • A single leading underscore, as in _tools, marks an attribute or method as internal: other modules should not use it. Python does not block the access; the underscore is an agreement between programmers, and PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 8 calls it a weak “internal use” indicator.
  • Two leading underscores, as in __secret, trigger name mangling: Python renames the attribute _ClassName__secret. The purpose is to avoid accidental name clashes in subclasses; it is not a protection mechanism.
  • A property without a setter gives read access to a computed value and refuses assignment with AttributeError (on a class that is not frozen: “property 'hours' of 'TimeEntry' object has no setter”). On our frozen TimeEntry, the frozen check answers first: first.hours = 2 raises FrozenInstanceError, a subclass of AttributeError.
  • frozen=True refuses every assignment to a field after creation, so the invariant cannot be broken by later code.

In the UML (Unified Modeling Language) class diagram of Lesson 5.3, the internal members appear with the symbol − (private) and the public ones with + (public).

▣ Slide 12 — __repr__ and __str__

__repr__ and __str__

Python asks an object for text in two situations. repr(obj) calls __repr__, which should return an unambiguous text for developers, ideally the expression that recreates the object; @dataclass writes it. str(obj) and print(obj) call __str__, which should return a readable text for people; when a class defines no __str__, Python uses __repr__. Our TimeEntry adds a short __str__:

>>> repr(first)
"TimeEntry(date=datetime.date(2026, 9, 14), staff_id='S1', routine='email_triage', category='communication', start_hour=9, minutes=36, interruptions=1, tool='manual', done=True)"
>>> print(first)
2026-09-14 S1 email_triage: 36 min (manual)
The developer view (generated __repr__) and the user view (our __str__).
Where this goes in JARVIS
TimeEntry is the first class of jarvis/models.py (Brick 5). In Class 6, StatsEngine and EconEngine receive lists of TimeEntry objects; in Brick 9, each of the three validation rules becomes a pytest test; and Part B of the Mid-Term (November 20) asks you to explain encapsulation on code like this.

▣ Slide 15 — Real-life example 5.1 — one row, one checked object
Real-life example 5.1

Turning one row of the time log into a checked object

The task of this example
Create TimeEntry objects for two real rows of boreal_routines_2026.csv — S1's manual e-mail triage of September 14 (36 minutes) and S1's first assistant-triaged run of September 25 (19 minutes) — compute their cost at 28 $/h, and show that two damaged rows (−19 minutes, tool jarvs) are refused and that an object cannot be changed after creation.
How it relates to Lesson 5.1
The example applies every concept of Lesson 5.1 to one real row: class and object, @dataclass, the generated __init__/__repr__/__eq__, validation in __post_init__, a method with a parameter, two properties, __str__ and frozen=True.

Boréal Studio's office manager keeps the time log and asks a precise question before the studio trusts any number: “If someone types −19 minutes by mistake, will that row end up in the monthly cost report?”

With TimeEntry the answer is no. The object is never created, the reason is reported in plain words, and every object that does exist satisfies the three rules for as long as the program runs. The two valid runs cost 16.80 $ (36 / 60 × 28) and 8.87 $ (19 / 60 × 28); the pilot run is the first row of the comparison you computed in Class 4.

Deliverables of the example
  • jarvis/models.py with TimeEntry: nine fields, three checks, cost(), hours, is_automated, __str__
  • The two costs checked by hand: 16.80 $ and 8.87 $
  • The three rejection messages, written down: they become three pytest tests
Where it returns in the course (future Bricks)
  • Brick 5 (due Oct 29) — jarvis/models.py, tag alpha-0.1
  • Brick 6 (due Nov 5) — EconEngine.routine_cost uses TimeEntry.cost
  • Brick 9 (due Dec 3) — tests with pytest.raises(ValueError)

Boréal Studio is a fictional teaching case; its data are synthetic (section 6.7, data and privacy).

    Step-by-step explanation of the program
    1. Lines 11–18. The program imports dataclass and FrozenInstanceError, then defines two constants: the set ALLOWED_TOOLS and HOURLY_VALUE = 28.0. Constants are written in UPPER_CASE (PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 8).
    2. Lines 22–84. Python executes the class statement once. The class body records nine annotated fields and five methods; then @dataclass(frozen=True) writes __init__, __repr__, __eq__, __hash__ and the __setattr__ that refuses changes. No TimeEntry object exists yet: only the class.
    3. Line 90. TimeEntry(date(2026, 9, 14), "S1", ..., True) passes nine positional arguments in field order. The generated __init__ stores them, then calls __post_init__: the visualization shows the three checks turning green.
    4. Lines 92–94. repr(first) prints the developer view written by @dataclass; print(first) calls our __str__ and prints 2026-09-14 S1 email_triage: 36 min (manual).
    5. Lines 96–98. first.cost(HOURLY_VALUE) computes 36 / 60 × 28 = 16.80; first.hours (0.60) and first.is_automated (False) are read without parentheses because they are properties.
    6. Lines 100–102. A second object of the same class: the pilot run, 19 minutes with the tool jarvis, costs 8.87 $ and is_automated is True. The two objects keep separate values.
    7. Lines 104–118. The loop tries the two damaged rows. The first fails the check minutes >= 0, the second fails the check on the tool; each ValueError is caught by except and printed, and the loop continues.
    8. Lines 120–126. first.minutes = 20 raises FrozenInstanceError: cannot assign to field 'minutes'; the value 36 is unchanged.
    9. Lines 128–130. same has the same nine values as first: first == same is True (the generated __eq__ compares fields) but first is same is False (two different objects in memory).

    Flash cards — Lesson 5.1
    Click or press Enter on a card to see its back.
    Card 5.1.1What is the difference between a class and an object?
    AnswerA class is the definition: attributes and methods. An object is one instance created from it, with its own values. TimeEntry is a class; first and pilot are two objects of it.
    Card 5.1.2Which methods does @dataclass write for TimeEntry, and what does frozen=True add?
    Answer__init__, __repr__ and __eq__, from the nine annotated fields. frozen=True makes any assignment to a field raise FrozenInstanceError and, with eq=True, also generates __hash__.
    Card 5.1.3When does __post_init__ run, and what is it used for in TimeEntry?
    AnswerRight after the generated __init__ has stored the fields. It checks minutes ≥ 0, 0 ≤ start_hour ≤ 23 and a known tool, and raises ValueError, so an invalid object is never created.
    Card 5.1.4What do print(first) and repr(first) show?
    Answerprint() uses __str__: 2026-09-14 S1 email_triage: 36 min (manual). repr() uses the generated __repr__: TimeEntry(date=datetime.date(2026, 9, 14), staff_id='S1', …, done=True).
    Card 5.1.5How does Python express “private”, and what is a property?
    AnswerBy convention: _name marks a member as internal (nothing enforces it); __name triggers name mangling. A property (@property) is a method read like an attribute: first.hours gives 0.6.

    Collections and CSV (Comma-Separated Values) parsing: from the file to list[TimeEntry]Collections & CSV (Comma-Separated Values) parsing
    ⏱ 0:15–0:26 · activity 0:26–0:30
    ▣ Slide 17 — 5.2 Collections & CSV (Comma-Separated Values) parsing — key terms
    Collections and CSV (Comma-Separated Values) parsing: from the file to list[TimeEntry]
    Objective of Lesson 5.2 · 0:15–0:26
    Read the whole dataset into a list[TimeEntry] with csv.DictReader and pathlib, convert every text value to its Python type, skip and report a bad row instead of crashing, and group the objects with defaultdict.
    Key terms
    Collection
    An object that contains other objects. The four built-in collections used in JARVIS are list, dict, set and tuple.
    list
    An ordered, changeable sequence that may contain the same value several times; positions start at 0. entries: list[TimeEntry].
    dict
    A mapping from unique keys to values. Keys must be hashable; a dict keeps the order in which keys were inserted (guaranteed since Python 3.7).
    set
    An unordered collection of unique, hashable values with a fast membership test ("jarvis" in ALLOWED_TOOLS).
    tuple
    An ordered sequence that cannot be changed after creation; used for a fixed group of values such as (line_no, reason).
    CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file
    A text file in which each line is one record and commas separate the fields; the first line, the header, usually holds the column names.
    csv.DictReader
    A reader of the standard-library module csv that returns each data line as a dict mapping the column names of the header to text values.
    pathlib.Path
    An object that represents a file-system path. The operator / joins parts with the separator of the operating system.
    Absolute and relative path
    An absolute path starts at the root of one computer (C:\Users\…, /home/…); a relative path is built from a known folder, here the folder of the program.
    Context manager (with)
    An object that prepares a resource at the start of a with block and releases it at the end, even after an error; an open file is closed automatically.
    Type conversion
    Turning a value of one type into another: int("36") gives 36, date.fromisoformat("2026-09-14") gives date(2026, 9, 14).
    Exception
    An object that signals an error and interrupts the normal order of execution: ValueError (right type, wrong value), TypeError (wrong type, such as None), KeyError (missing key).
    try / except
    A statement that runs a block and, if one of the named exceptions occurs, runs the handler instead of stopping the program.
    defaultdict
    A dict subclass of the module collections that creates a default value, such as an empty list, the first time a missing key is used.
    Counter
    A dict subclass of the module collections that counts how many times each value appears.
    ▣ Slide 18 — Four collections, four jobs
    Four collections, four jobs
    A collection is an object that contains other objects. Each of the four built-in collections has properties that make it the right choice for one job of the loader:
    Table 5.2.A — The four built-in collections and their job in the loaderCSV
    TypeOrderedChangeableDuplicatesJob in JARVIS
    listyesyesallowedentries: the 420 TimeEntry objects, in file order
    dictinsertion orderyeskeys uniqueone CSV (Comma-Separated Values) row: {"date": "2026-09-14", "staff_id": "S1", …}
    setnoyesnoALLOWED_TOOLS; the staff IDs (identifiers) {"S1", …, "S5"}
    tupleyesnoallowedone skipped line: (4, "invalid literal for int() with base 10: '17.0'")
    Two choices deserve a reason. ALLOWED_TOOLS is a set because the loader asks one question about it, “is this tool in the collection?”, and a set answers that question in constant average time without scanning its elements; it also cannot hold the same tool twice. A skipped line is a tuple because the pair (line number, reason) is a fixed record that nobody should modify after the fact.
    ▣ Slide 19 — Paths: pathlib, never a hard-coded path
    Paths: pathlib, never a hard-coded path
    A path such as C:\Users\ana\Desktop\boreal.csv works on one computer only. It fails on a teammate's Mac, on the Linux server that runs your GitHub Actions workflow, and on the projector computer during the defense, where the course requires “a fresh clone that runs in under two minutes”. The rubric lists “hard-coded paths” under Developing for the Lab Proficiency dimension. The module pathlib (Python 3.4, PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 428) builds every path from the location of the program:
    from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent      # the folder that contains this .py file
DATA = HERE.parent / "data"                 # the data folder next to the code folder
csv_path = DATA / "boreal_routines_2026.csv"
    __file__ is the path of the running program; resolve() makes it absolute; / joins two parts with the right separator.
    ▣ Slide 20 — Opening the file and csv.DictReader
    Opening the file correctly
    The loader opens the file with with path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:. Each part of this line has a reason. The with statement uses the file as a context manager: the file is closed when the block ends, even if an exception occurs inside it. newline="" is what the documentation of the csv module requires, so that the module itself handles the line endings of the file. encoding="utf-8" reads the text with the UTF-8 (8-bit Unicode Transformation Format) encoding on every operating system; without it, Windows may use a different default encoding and read the letter é of “Boréal” incorrectly.
    csv.DictReader: one dict of strings per line
    csv.DictReader(f) reads the first line as the header and returns every following line as a dict whose keys are the column names. For line 2 of the dataset the result is {"date": "2026-09-14", "staff_id": "S1", "routine": "email_triage", "category": "communication", "start_hour": "9", "minutes": "36", "interruptions": "1", "tool": "manual", "done": "1"}. Every value is a str, including "36": the reader never guesses types. Three behaviours of the reader matter for a loader:
    • reader.fieldnames is the list of column names of the header. The loader compares it with the nine required names (a set difference) and stops with a clear message if a column is missing: a wrong file is not a bad row.
    • A line with more values than the header (a trailing comma, for example) keeps the extra values in a list stored under the key None (the parameter restkey, whose default is None).
    • A line with fewer values than the header receives None for the missing keys (the parameter restval). Completely empty lines are skipped by the reader.
    ▣ Slide 21 — Converting text — and what fails (1/2)
    ▣ Slide 22 — Converting text — and what fails (2/2)
    Converting text, and what fails
    Every conversion either produces a value of the right type or raises an exception. The loader relies on this: it does not test each value in advance, it converts and handles the failure. This style has a name in the Python glossary, EAFP (Easier to Ask for Forgiveness than Permission): try the operation and handle the exception, instead of checking every condition first (the opposite style is LBYL (Look Before You Leap)).
    Table 5.2.B — Conversions used by the loader and their failures (Python 3.12 and later)CSV
    Text in the fileConversionResult
    "36"int()36
    " 36 "int()36 (surrounding spaces are accepted)
    "17.0"int()ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '17.0'
    "" (empty cell)int()ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: ''
    None (missing field)int()TypeError: int() argument must be a string, …, not 'NoneType'
    "2026-09-14"date.fromisoformat()date(2026, 9, 14)
    "2026/09/14"date.fromisoformat()ValueError: Invalid isoformat string: '2026/09/14'
    "1"== "1"True
    The date format of the dataset, yyyy-mm-dd, is the calendar date format of the international standard ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 8601 (official page of the standard); date.fromisoformat reads it directly. int("17.0") fails because int() accepts only the text of a whole number: "17.0" is the text of a decimal number. int(float("17.0")) would give 17, but it would also turn "17.9" into 17 without any warning, so the loader rejects the value and the person who exported the file corrects the cell.
    ▣ Slide 23 — try/except: report the row, never crash
    try/except: report the row, never crash
    for line_no, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):      # line 1 of the file is the header
    try:
        entries.append(self._parse_row(row))            # conversion + TimeEntry checks
    except (ValueError, TypeError) as err:
        self.skipped.append((line_no, str(err)))        # keep the line number and the reason
    The loop of DataLoader.load: one bad line is recorded, the next line is read.
    The handler catches only the two exceptions that a bad row can produce: ValueError (a text that cannot be converted, or a value refused by TimeEntry.__post_init__) and TypeError (a missing value, None). Any other exception, such as FileNotFoundError, still stops the program, because it signals a setup problem and not a data problem. enumerate(reader, start=2) numbers the records from 2, because line 1 is the header; in our exports, which contain no blank line and no field written over several lines, the record number is the line number, so the report says “line 4” and the office manager can find the cell. In a file with blank lines (which DictReader skips) the two would drift apart; reader.line_num then gives the physical line number of the record just read. On the damaged sample the loader returns 8 objects and 4 skipped lines; on the full dataset it returns 420 objects and 0 skipped lines.
    ▣ Slide 24 — Grouping with defaultdict, counting with Counter
    Grouping with defaultdict, counting with Counter
    from collections import Counter, defaultdict

minutes_by_routine = defaultdict(list)
for entry in entries:
    minutes_by_routine[entry.routine].append(entry.minutes)   # 6 keys x 70 values

Counter(entry.tool for entry in entries)    # {'manual': 370, 'template': 35, 'jarvis': 15}
    defaultdict(list) creates an empty list the first time a key is used; Counter counts the values.
    With an ordinary dict, the loop would need two more lines: if entry.routine not in d: d[entry.routine] = []. The defaultdict calls list() for a missing key and stores the new empty list before the append. The result has six keys, one per routine, each with 70 values (14 days × 5 staff members). Counter gives the number of runs per tool: 370 manual, 35 with the report template (7 days × 5 staff members) and 15 with JARVIS (5 days × S1, S2, S3). These groups are exactly the input of StatsEngine and EconEngine in Class 6.
    Where this goes in JARVIS
    jarvis/loader.py with DataLoader.load(path) -> list[TimeEntry] is part of Brick 5, and python -m jarvis load must print the row count, the skipped count and the first three entries. The grouping per routine, per staff member and per day is the first task of Brick 6; the three bad-input cases of Brick 10 (bad rows, empty file, unknown routine) start from this code.

    ▣ Slide 27 — Real-life example 5.2 — four damaged lines
    Real-life example 5.2
    Loading a log export that contains four damaged lines
    The task of this example
    Load the twelve rows of September 14 that the office manager exported (routines_sample_broken.csv), four of them damaged — a decimal 17.0, a trailing comma, a date typed 2026/09/14 and a sign typo -19 — report each bad line with its number and reason without stopping; then load the full 420-row dataset with the same loader, print the first three entries, group the minutes per routine and count the runs per tool.
    How it relates to Lesson 5.2
    The example applies every concept of Lesson 5.2: the four collections, pathlib, with, csv.DictReader, type conversion, try/except with ValueError and TypeError, defaultdict(list) and Counter; the checks of Lesson 5.1 reject the negative duration.
    Every Friday Boréal Studio's office manager exports the week's log from a shared spreadsheet. Spreadsheets change cells without asking: a number formatted with one decimal becomes 17.0, a date typed by hand becomes 2026/09/14, an extra empty column adds a trailing comma, and a missed key gives −19 minutes.
    JARVIS must load what is correct, say exactly what is wrong and where, and never stop. The result on the sample is “loaded 8, skipped 4” with four reasons; on the full dataset it is “loaded 420, skipped 0”.
    Deliverables of the example
    • jarvis/loader.py with DataLoader.load(path) -> list[TimeEntry] and the skipped report
    • The console report: sample: loaded 8, skipped 4 and the four reasons with their line numbers
    • full file: loaded 420, skipped 0 and the first three entries — the output of python -m jarvis load
    • The grouped minutes (6 routines × 70 runs) and the runs per tool (370 / 35 / 15)
    Where it returns in the course (future Bricks)
    • Brick 5 (due Oct 29) — loader.py and python -m jarvis load
    • Brick 6 (due Nov 5) — grouping per routine, staff member and day; the Store imports the entries
    • Brick 10 (due Dec 10) — three bad-input cases demonstrated, never a crash
    • Mid-Term Part B (Nov 20) — read and complete code like loader.py
    Boréal Studio is a fictional teaching case; its data are synthetic (section 6.7, data and privacy).

      Step-by-step explanation of the program
      1. Lines 12–26. The program imports csv, Counter, defaultdict, date, Path and TimeEntry (from time_entry.py of Lesson 5.1), then builds HERE and DATA from the location of the file: no path is typed by hand.
      2. Lines 30–40. The class DataLoader has one class attribute, REQUIRED (the nine column names), and __init__ gives each loader object its own empty list skipped.
      3. Lines 43–69. _parse_row is a static method (it needs no self) and is internal (leading underscore). It rejects a row that contains the key None, then converts each field: date.fromisoformat, int() three times, a comparison for done. If every conversion succeeds, TimeEntry(...) runs the three checks of Lesson 5.1.
      4. Lines 72–86. load resets the report, opens the file with with, creates the DictReader and stops at once if a required column is missing from the header.
      5. Lines 88–96. The loop numbers the data lines from 2. For each line it tries _parse_row; a ValueError or a TypeError is caught and recorded as (line_no, reason). Replay line 4 (17.0), line 6 (trailing comma), line 9 (2026/09/14) and line 11 (-19, refused by __post_init__).
      6. Line 98. The with block has closed the file; load returns the list of eight objects.

      8. Lines 114–120. The same loader object loads the full file: 420 objects, 0 skipped lines. The first three objects are printed with TimeEntry.__str__.
      9. Lines 122–134. defaultdict(list) collects the minutes of each routine (6 × 70); Counter counts the tools (370 / 35 / 15); a set comprehension lists the five staff IDs (identifiers) once each.

      Card 5.2.1What does csv.DictReader return for each data line, and what type are the values?
      AnswerA dict whose keys are the column names of the header and whose values are all str: "36" stays text until int() converts it.
      Card 5.2.2Why build the path with Path(__file__).resolve().parent instead of typing "C:\Users\ana\Desktop\boreal.csv"?
      AnswerThe path starts from the folder of the program, so it works on every computer and operating system, in GitHub Actions and at the defense. A hard-coded path works on one machine only.
      Card 5.2.3What does int("17.0") do, and why?
      AnswerIt raises ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '17.0'. int() accepts only the text of a whole number; "17.0" is the text of a decimal number.
      Card 5.2.4What does DictReader do with a line that has one value more than the header (a trailing comma)?
      AnswerIt stores the surplus values in a list under the key None. Our loader detects None in row and skips the line with the reason “more fields than the header”.
      Card 5.2.5What does defaultdict(list) do in minutes_by_routine[entry.routine].append(entry.minutes)?
      AnswerThe first time a routine name is used as a key, it creates and stores an empty list, so append always works. Result: six keys with 70 values each.

      Responsibilities → classes → UML (Unified Modeling Language): designing JARVIS before coding itResponsibilities → classes → UML (Unified Modeling Language)
      ⏱ 0:30–0:41 · activity 0:41–0:45
      ▣ Slide 29 — 5.3 Responsibilities → classes → UML (Unified Modeling Language) — key terms
      Responsibilities → classes → UML (Unified Modeling Language): designing JARVIS before coding it
      Objective of Lesson 5.3 · 0:30–0:41
      Give each requirement of JARVIS to exactly one class, place the classes in modules, and draw and read a UML (Unified Modeling Language) class diagram with visibility, relationships and multiplicity.
      Key terms
      Responsibility
      Something a class must know (information it keeps) or do (an operation it performs) for the system.
      Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
      A class should have one responsibility; in Robert C. Martin's wording, a module should have one, and only one, reason to change.
      Cohesion
      How closely the members of one class belong together. High cohesion: every attribute and method serves the same responsibility.
      Coupling
      How much a class depends on other classes. Low coupling: a change in one class rarely forces a change in another.
      CRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) card
      An index card with three areas — class name, responsibilities, collaborators (the classes it works with) — introduced by Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham in 1989 to test a design before coding it.
      Module and package
      A module is one .py file; a package is a folder of modules with an __init__.py file. jarvis/ is the package of the project.
      UML (Unified Modeling Language)
      The standard graphical language for software models, maintained by the Object Management Group (OMG); the current formal version is 2.5.1 (December 2017).
      Class diagram
      A UML (Unified Modeling Language) diagram that shows classes as boxes with three compartments (name, attributes, operations) and the relationships between them.
      Visibility
      The symbol in front of a member: + public, − private, # protected, ~ package.
      Association
      A structural link between objects of two classes, drawn as a solid line; an arrowhead shows the direction in which one object knows the other (navigability).
      Aggregation
      A whole–part association in which the part can exist without the whole; drawn with a hollow diamond at the whole.
      Composition
      A whole–part association in which the part belongs to one whole at a time and is deleted with it; drawn with a filled diamond at the whole.
      Dependency
      One class uses another temporarily (as a parameter, a local variable or a return value); drawn as a dashed arrow.
      Generalization (inheritance)
      The subclass is a specialized kind of its superclass; drawn as a solid line with a hollow triangle at the superclass.
      Multiplicity
      The number of objects at one end of a relationship: 1, 0..1, * (same as 0..*), 1..*.
      ▣ Slide 30 — From requirements to responsibilities
      From requirements to responsibilities
      In Brick 2 you wrote user stories; in Bricks 3 and 4 you wrote the signatures of the economics and statistics methods. Design is the step that decides where each piece of that work will live in the program. A responsibility is something a class must know or do. The method is short: read each requirement, ask which object should know this or do this, and give the requirement to exactly one class.
      The rule that guides the choice is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP): a class should have one responsibility, or, in the formulation of Robert C. Martin, one reason to change. Two measurable consequences follow. Cohesion is high when every member of a class serves the same responsibility; coupling is low when a change in one class rarely forces a change in another. A class that publishes the dashboard and also runs the agent loop changes whenever either job changes: two reasons to change, low cohesion.
      A quick way to test a design with your team before drawing anything is the CRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) card, introduced by Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham at the OOPSLA (Object-Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages & Applications) '89 conference: one index card per class, with the class name, its responsibilities and the classes it collaborates with. On a CRC card the word responsibility means one item the class knows or does; the SRP (Single Responsibility Principle) asks that all the items of one class serve a single purpose, so that the class has one reason to change. A card that needs more than three or four items usually mixes purposes: split the class.

      ▣ Slide 33 — Reading a UML (Unified Modeling Language) class box
      Reading a UML (Unified Modeling Language) class box
      The Unified Modeling Language (UML) is the standard notation for software models; its specification is published by the Object Management Group (OMG), currently in version 2.5.1. A class is drawn as a box with three compartments: the class name; the attributes, written visibility name: type; and the operations, written visibility name(parameter: type): return type.

│                DataLoader                │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ + skipped: list[tuple[int, str]]         │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ + load(path: Path): list[TimeEntry]      │
│ − _parse_row(row: dict): TimeEntry       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
      The DataLoader of Lesson 5.2 as a UML (Unified Modeling Language) class box: name, one public attribute, one public and one private operation.

      ▣ Slide 34 — Relationships between classes
      Relationships between classes
      • Association — a solid line: objects of one class keep a link to objects of another. Agent → Store (“logs runs in”): the agent keeps a reference to the store. The arrowhead shows the direction of navigation.
      • Aggregation — a hollow diamond at the whole: a whole–part association in which the part can exist without the whole. Agent ◇— Tool: main() creates the tools and passes them to the agent, so each tool exists before and independently of the agent, and a test can pass a different tool.
      • Composition — a filled diamond at the whole: the part belongs to one whole at a time and is deleted with it (UML (Unified Modeling Language) 2.5.1 does not require the whole to create the part). If Agent.__init__ contained self._provider = OfflineProvider(), the provider would be created by the agent and would live only inside it: a composition. JARVIS avoids this on purpose, so that a test, or the ApiProvider of Class 10, can be passed in instead.
      • Dependency — a dashed arrow: one class uses another for a moment, as a parameter, a local variable or a return value. DataLoader ⇢ TimeEntry (“creates”): the loader builds entries and returns them without keeping them.
      • Generalization (inheritance) — a solid line with a hollow triangle at the parent: LogTimeTool —▷ Tool. A dashed line with a hollow triangle (realization) is used when the parent is a pure interface; in Python Tool is a class, so the solid line is the usual reading.
      ▣ Slide 35 — Multiplicity
      Multiplicity
      Multiplicity states how many objects take part at one end of a relationship. 1 means exactly one; 0..1 zero or one; * (written also 0..*) any number, zero included; 1..* at least one. Each end is read from the other side: Agent "1" ◇— "1..*" Tool reads “one agent holds one or more tools”; Store "1" — "0..*" TimeEntry reads “one store keeps zero or more entries” — an empty database is a valid state.
      ▣ Slide 36 — Drawing the diagram: draw.io, PlantUML or paper
      Drawing the diagram
      Three tools are accepted for Brick 5: draw.io (diagrams.net), which draws the boxes by hand in the browser; PlantUML, which turns a text description into a diagram; or a clean drawing on paper, photographed. PlantUML has an advantage for a team: the text file docs/uml.puml is versioned in Git with the code, and a change to the design appears in the commit history like any other change.
      @startuml
skinparam classAttributeIconSize 0
abstract class Tool {
  + name: str
  + run(args: dict, store: Store): str {abstract}
}
Tool <|-- LogTimeTool
Agent "1" o-- "1..*" Tool : dispatches to
Agent "1" --> "1" Store : logs runs in
DataLoader ..> TimeEntry : creates
@enduml

      Boréal Studio's owner adds a requirement after reading the Brick 2 proposal: “I want a dashboard, with aggregated numbers only.” A first draft gives it to the Agent, because the agent already sees every request.
      The design check finds the Agent with two requirements, R11 (choose the tool and record every run) and R12 (publish the dashboard): two reasons to change. R12 moves to the Reporter. The corrected design has 16 classes in 12 modules, two abstract classes and 16 relationships, and the program writes it as a 102-line PlantUML file.

        Flash cards — Lesson 5.3
        Click or press Enter on a card to see its back.
        Card 5.3.1What does the Single Responsibility Principle say, and how is it checked in JARVIS?
        AnswerA class should have one responsibility — one reason to change. Each requirement goes to exactly one class; a class that collects two unrelated requirements is split, or one requirement moves (R12: Agent → Reporter).
        Card 5.3.2What are the three compartments of a UML (Unified Modeling Language) class box?
        AnswerThe class name; the attributes (visibility name: type); the operations (visibility name(parameter: type): return type).
        Card 5.3.3What is the difference between aggregation and composition?
        AnswerBoth are whole–part associations. Aggregation (hollow diamond): the part can exist without the whole, like the Tools passed to the Agent. Composition (filled diamond): the part belongs to one whole at a time and is deleted with it.
        Card 5.3.4How do you read Agent "1" o-- "1..*" Tool?
        AnswerOne Agent aggregates one or more Tools. A Tool exists outside the Agent: main() creates it and passes it in.
        Card 5.3.5How does UML (Unified Modeling Language) show that LogTimeTool inherits from Tool, and that Tool is abstract?
        AnswerA solid line from LogTimeTool to Tool with a hollow triangle at Tool (generalization). Tool's name is written in italics, or marked {abstract}.
        Activity 3 cards — the six UML (Unified Modeling Language) symbols
        Activity 3 · card 1UML (Unified Modeling Language) symbol −
        AnswerPrivate member. In Python: one leading underscore, by convention. Example: − _path: Path in Store.
        Activity 3 · card 2UML (Unified Modeling Language) symbol +
        AnswerPublic member. Example: + load(path: Path): list[TimeEntry] in DataLoader.
        Activity 3 · card 3Association
        AnswerA solid line: objects of one class keep a link to objects of another; the arrowhead shows navigability. Example: Agent → Store (logs runs in).
        Activity 3 · card 4Aggregation
        AnswerA hollow diamond at the whole: a whole–part link in which the part can exist without the whole. Example: Agent ◇— Tool.
        Activity 3 · card 5Inherits (generalization)
        AnswerA solid line with a hollow triangle at the parent: the subclass is a kind of its parent. Example: LogTimeTool —▷ Tool.
        Activity 3 · card 6Multiplicity 1..*
        AnswerAt least one, with no upper limit. Example: one Agent holds one or more Tools.

        Abstract base classes, polymorphism and clean-code habitsABCs (Abstract Base Classes), polymorphism & clean code
        ⏱ 0:45–0:56 · activity 0:56–1:00
        ▣ Slide 41 — 5.4 ABCs (Abstract Base Classes), polymorphism & clean code — key terms
        Abstract base classes, polymorphism and clean-code habits
        Objective of Lesson 5.4 · 0:45–0:56
        Define Tool and Provider as abstract base classes, write subclasses that override their methods, explain polymorphism in the agent loop, and recognize the code smells that cost marks.
        Key terms
        Inheritance
        A subclass receives the attributes and methods of its superclass and can add new ones or replace them: class LogTimeTool(Tool):.
        Superclass and subclass
        The superclass (base class, parent) is the class inherited from; the subclass (derived class, child) is the class that inherits.
        Overriding
        A subclass defines a method with the same name and parameters as a method of its superclass; for objects of the subclass, the subclass version runs.
        Abstract base class (ABC)
        A class that declares methods its subclasses must implement and that cannot be instantiated itself; in Python it inherits from abc.ABC.
        @abstractmethod
        The decorator of the module abc that marks a method as abstract. A class that still has an unimplemented abstract method cannot be instantiated: Python raises TypeError.
        Concrete class
        A class in which every abstract method has an implementation, so objects can be created from it: LogTimeTool, OfflineProvider.
        Polymorphism
        The same call — tool.run(args, store), provider.parse(text) — executes different code depending on the class of the object that receives it.
        Dependency injection
        Passing the objects a class needs (provider, tools, store) as parameters of its constructor instead of creating them inside the class.
        Regular expression
        A pattern that describes text; re.compile(r"log\s+(\d+)\s*min\s+(\w+)") finds “log 25 min email_triage” and captures 25 and email_triage.
        Code smell
        A surface sign in the code that usually points to a deeper problem (Martin Fowler): a secret in the code, a hard-coded path, a 200-line function.
        PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 8
        The official style guide for Python code: indentation, line length (79 characters), naming conventions, blank lines, imports.
        Docstring
        A string literal written as the first statement of a module, class or function to document it (PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 257).
        Mutable default argument
        A default value such as [] or {}: it is created once, when def runs, and shared by every call that does not pass the argument.
        Environment variable
        A named value in the environment of a running program, read with os.environ.get("JARVIS_API_KEY"); the right place for a secret.
        ▣ Slide 42 — Inheritance and overriding
        Inheritance and overriding
        Inheritance lets a class reuse the definition of another class. In class LogTimeTool(Tool):, Tool is the superclass and LogTimeTool the subclass: the subclass receives the class attributes name and description and the method run, and it overrides run with its own version. The test for inheritance is the sentence “a LogTimeTool is a Tool”. The sentence “an Agent is a Tool” is false, so the Agent does not inherit from Tool; an agent has tools, which is the aggregation of Lesson 5.3.
        class LogTimeTool(Tool):
    """Records the minutes of one routine run."""

    name = "log_time"
    description = "log the minutes spent on one routine"

    def run(self, args: dict, store: MemoryStore) -> str:
        store.entries.append({"routine": args["routine"], "minutes": args["minutes"]})
        return f"logged {args['minutes']} min of {args['routine']}"
        A concrete tool: two class attributes that replace the empty ones of Tool, and an overriding run().
        ▣ Slide 43 — Abstract base classes: Tool and Provider
        Abstract base classes
        Tool itself must never be used as a tool: it only states what every tool has. An abstract base class (ABC) expresses this in code. The class inherits from ABC (module abc, introduced by PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 3119), and the method that every subclass must write is marked @abstractmethod; its body is only the docstring.
        from abc import ABC, abstractmethod


class Tool(ABC):
    """One action the assistant can perform; subclasses must implement run()."""

    name: str = ""
    description: str = ""

    @abstractmethod
    def run(self, args: dict, store: MemoryStore) -> str:
        """Perform the action with the given arguments and return a reply for the user."""


class Provider(ABC):
    """Turns a text request into an Intent; subclasses must implement parse()."""

    @abstractmethod
    def parse(self, text: str) -> Intent:
        """Return the Intent of the request."""
        The two abstract base classes of JARVIS. Intent is a frozen dataclass with two fields: name and args.
        Python refuses to create an object of a class that still has an unimplemented abstract method. Tool() raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Tool without an implementation for abstract method 'run'. The same happens to a subclass that forgets the method: SummarizeTool, planned for Class 10, has a name but no run(), so SummarizeTool() fails in the same way. The value of the mechanism is the moment of the error: it appears when the object is created, on the developer's computer, instead of later, during a demo, when a user sends the first request that needs the missing method.
        ▣ Slide 44 — Polymorphism in the agent loop
        ▣ Slide 45 — Dependency injection — and what the rubric says
        Polymorphism in the agent loop
        class Agent:
    """Runs the loop request -> intent -> tool -> result -> log."""

    def __init__(self, provider: Provider, tools: list[Tool], store: MemoryStore) -> None:
        self._provider = provider
        self._tools = {tool.name: tool for tool in tools}
        self._store = store

    def handle(self, text: str) -> str:
        intent = self._provider.parse(text)              # polymorphism: any Provider subclass
        tool = self._tools.get(intent.name)
        if tool is None:
            self._store.runs.append((text, intent.name, "none"))
            return f"sorry, no tool for {text!r}"
        reply = tool.run(intent.args, self._store)       # polymorphism: any Tool subclass
        self._store.runs.append((text, intent.name, type(tool).__name__))
        return reply
        Agent.handle never asks which class it is working with.
        Polymorphism means that one call executes different code depending on the class of the object. In handle(), tool.run(intent.args, self._store) runs LogTimeTool.run for “log 25 min email_triage”, AddTaskTool.run for “add task call the accountant” and DailyReportTool.run for “report”. The agent contains no if intent.name == "log_time": … elif … chain. The consequences are measurable. Adding SummarizeTool in Class 10 means writing one subclass, teaching the provider one more request pattern (a rule of OfflineProvider, or the ApiProvider) and adding one object to the list in main(); the Agent class does not change. Replacing OfflineProvider by ApiProvider means changing one argument in main(); again the Agent does not change.
        This works because the agent receives its provider, its tools and its store as constructor parameters: dependency injection. A test can pass a provider that always returns the same Intent, or a store that lives in memory, and test the agent alone. The OfflineProvider comes first in the course for the same reason: the tests, the Mid-Term and the defense must never depend on a network connection or an API (Application Programming Interface) key; the ApiProvider of Class 10 is one more subclass of Provider, with the offline provider as its fallback.
        What the rubric says
        Tech Implementation, level Exemplary (93–100 %): “advanced OOP (Object-Oriented Programming) (abstract base classes, polymorphism) used effectively”. Two abstract base classes, each implemented by several subclasses and used through one call in the agent, are exactly the evidence this level asks for. Level Developing (70–82 %) describes the opposite: “procedural style instead of OOP”.
        ▣ Slide 46 — Clean-code habits that cost or earn marks (1/2)
        ▣ Slide 47 — Clean-code habits that cost or earn marks (2/2)
        Clean-code habits that cost or earn marks
        A code smell, in Martin Fowler's definition, is a surface sign in the code that usually corresponds to a deeper problem. The habits below are checked in the code review of Sprint 1, in the Lab Proficiency dimension of the rubric, and by any reader of your repository:
        Table 5.4.A — Clean-code checklist used in the code reviewCSV
        HabitThe smell it preventsRule in JARVIS
        Follow PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 8inconsistent indentation, 150-character lines, names in mixed styles4 spaces; at most 79 characters per line of code and 72 for comments and docstrings; snake_case for functions and variables, CapWords for classes, UPPER_CASE for constants
        Type hints on public functions (PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 484)a reader cannot tell what a function accepts or returnsdef load(self, path: Path) -> list[TimeEntry]:
        A docstring on every module, class and public method (PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 257)code whose purpose must be guessedone sentence that states the responsibility
        Small functions, one job eachan 80-line function that loads, computes and printsif the docstring needs “and”, split the function
        Meaningful namesx1, x2, l, tmpminutes_manual, minutes_jarvis, line_no
        No secret in the codeAPI_KEY = "demo-key-…" committed to GitHubos.environ.get("JARVIS_API_KEY"), a git-ignored .env, a repository secret; a key committed once is replaced the same day
        No hard-coded pathC:\Users\ana\Desktop\log.csvPath(__file__).resolve().parent (Lesson 5.2)
        No mutable default argumentdef add(item, seen=[]): one list shared by every callseen=None, then seen = [] if seen is None else seen
        Catch only the exceptions you expectexcept: or except Exception: hides real bugsexcept (ValueError, TypeError) around the conversions
        A design that pytest can testhidden global state, objects created deep inside methodsinputs as parameters, results returned, dependencies injected
        About the length of the lines in this module's programs
        The four teaching programs of Class 5 break the 72-character limit for comments, and some of their lines exceed 79 characters, because every line of code is preceded by a complete explanatory comment written for this lesson. Your JARVIS code follows PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 8: wrap comments at 72 characters and code at 79 (a team may agree on up to 99 for code, as PEP 8 allows), and let a checker such as flake8 or Ruff report the long lines.
        The mutable default argument deserves a precise explanation, because the error is invisible in a single test. Python evaluates a default value once, when the def statement runs, not at each call. In def add(item, seen=[]), every call that omits seen receives the same list object, so values added by an earlier call appear in the result of the next one. The Python tutorial gives the same warning in its section on default argument values.
        Where this goes in JARVIS
        In Brick 5 you write tools/base.py and providers.py with the two abstract base classes (skeletons only). In Brick 7 you write OfflineProvider, LogTimeTool and AddTaskTool and wire them into the Agent, so that python -m jarvis "log 25 min email_triage" writes a row with no key and no network. In Brick 10 the ApiProvider arrives as one more subclass, and the clean-code table above becomes the checklist of the code-review swap.

        ▣ Slide 50 — Real-life example 5.4 — S2's morning requests
        Real-life example 5.4
        One request, the right tool: S2's morning requests
        The task of this example
        Build an Agent that receives five text requests from a staff member — “log 25 min email_triage”, “add task call the accountant”, “log 12 min standup_notes”, “report” and “book a flight” — and sends each one through an OfflineProvider and the matching Tool subclass, using only the abstract types Provider and Tool; record which class handled each request, and show that an unfinished tool (SummarizeTool) cannot even be created.
        How it relates to Lesson 5.4
        The example applies inheritance, overriding, abstract base classes, @abstractmethod, polymorphism, dependency injection, a regular expression, a frozen dataclass (Intent) and two clean-code rules (the key from the environment, private attributes with a leading underscore).
        At 8:40, before a client call, S2 types four short requests into JARVIS, and a fifth one that JARVIS was never built for: “book a flight”. The assistant must route each request to the right action, answer politely when no tool exists, and record every request in its own run log.
        The run log is JARVIS's own dataset: in Sprint 2 its rows give the “requests per day” and “time saved” numbers, and the free-quota check of the break-even model of Class 3. The program also reads the environment, but only to report whether JARVIS_API_KEY exists: in this version the agent always uses the offline provider (the ApiProvider arrives in Class 10) — the design guarantee that the demo works without a network.
        Deliverables of the example
        • tools/base.py (Tool, abstract) and providers.py (Provider, abstract) — the Brick 5 skeletons
        • OfflineProvider with its regular expression, LogTimeTool, AddTaskTool, DailyReportTool and the Agent
        • The five replies and the run log (request, intent, class that handled it)
        • The TypeError of SummarizeTool() — the first test of tests/test_tools.py
        Where it returns in the course (future Bricks)
        • Brick 5 (due Oct 29) — the two abstract base classes as skeletons
        • Brick 7 (due Nov 12) — OfflineProvider, Tool base class, two tools wired into the Agent
        • Brick 9 (due Dec 3) — tests for the tools and the provider
        • Brick 10 (due Dec 10) — ApiProvider as one more subclass, with the offline fallback; code-review swap
        • Final defense (Jan 22) — “polymorphic Tool and Provider” is evidence for the Exemplary level

          Step-by-step explanation of the program
          1. Lines 12–18. Imports: os for the environment, re for the regular expression, ABC and abstractmethod, and dataclass with field.
          2. Lines 22–47. Intent is a frozen dataclass (name, args); MemoryStore keeps three lists in memory and stands in for the SQLite Store of Class 6.
          3. Lines 50–128. Python creates the class objects. Tool(ABC) declares the abstract run; LogTimeTool, AddTaskTool and DailyReportTool override it; SummarizeTool does not, so it stays abstract.
          4. Lines 131–169. Provider(ABC) declares the abstract parse; OfflineProvider implements it with one regular expression and two text rules, and returns Intent("unknown", …) when no rule matches.
          5. Lines 172–203. Agent receives its dependencies in __init__ and keeps them in private attributes; handle() calls parse, looks the tool up by name, calls run, and logs the class that handled the request.
          6. Lines 208–214. SummarizeTool() raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class SummarizeTool without an implementation for abstract method 'run'; the message is printed.
          7. Lines 216–222. The key is read with os.environ.get only to report whether one exists; in Class 5 the agent is always built with an OfflineProvider (Class 10 adds the ApiProvider), three tool objects and the store created in main().
          8. Lines 224–228. Five requests pass through the same handle() call. Watch the visualization: the provider is always OfflineProvider, but the class that runs changes — LogTimeTool, AddTaskTool, LogTimeTool, DailyReportTool — and “book a flight” gets the polite refusal.
          9. Lines 230–232. main() reads the run log through its own reference to the store, never through agent._store: five rows, one per request.

          Flash cards — Lesson 5.4
          Click or press Enter on a card to see its back.
          Card 5.4.1What is an abstract base class, and what does Tool() do?
          AnswerA class that declares methods its subclasses must implement (@abstractmethod) and that cannot be instantiated itself. Tool() raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Tool without an implementation for abstract method 'run'.
          Card 5.4.2Where is the polymorphism in Agent.handle()?
          AnswerIn the calls self._provider.parse(text) and tool.run(intent.args, self._store): each executes the code of the subclass of the object — LogTimeTool, AddTaskTool or DailyReportTool — without any if/elif on the tool name.
          Card 5.4.3Why does the Agent receive its provider, tools and store as parameters?
          AnswerDependency injection: main() or a test decides which objects to use. A test can pass a fake provider; Class 10 passes an ApiProvider instead of the OfflineProvider without changing the Agent.
          Card 5.4.4What is wrong with def add(item, seen=[])?
          AnswerThe default list is created once, when def runs, and shared by every call that omits seen, so earlier values reappear. Write seen=None and create a new list inside the function.
          Card 5.4.5Where does the API (Application Programming Interface) key belong, and where must it never be?
          AnswerIn an environment variable (os.environ.get("JARVIS_API_KEY")), a git-ignored .env file and a GitHub repository secret. Never in the code or in any committed file; a key committed once is replaced the same day.

          ▣ Slide 53 — Mid-Term (Nov 20): format and allowed materials
          Announcement — the Mid-Term format and the allowed materials
          • Date: Friday, November 20, 2026 — 30 % of the final grade, individual, in class, 120 minutes.
          • Part A — Computational (≈ 60 min): routine cost, marginal benefit and marginal cost, break-even hours, payback, mean, median, mode, sample SD (standard deviation), correlation and a before/after comparison, on a new slice of the routines data.
          • Part B — Application (≈ 60 min): complete or fix a Python method, explain a UML (Unified Modeling Language) fragment (why Tool is an abstract base class, one association), write two user stories and one research question.
          • Allowed materials: one handwritten Formula Card and one handwritten Design Card (one page each), a pen and a calculator. No laptop, no phone.
          • Your Design Card is today's work: the class diagram and one sentence of responsibility per class.
          ▣ Slide 54 — Home work and next class
          2 h
          Home work and next class
          1. Finish Brick 5; complete the README.md section “How to run”: python -m venv .venv, pip install -r requirements.txt, python -m jarvis load — relative paths only.
          2. Write docs/design.md (one page at most): why these classes, what each one owns, which classes are abstract and why.
          3. Skim Leedy & Ormrod, Chapter 5, Writing the Research Proposal (20 minutes).
          4. Weekly Progress Report #5. From this week, also log the hours you spend on JARVIS setup: they are the setup cost of the economic model of Brick 3.
          Next class — Class 6, Friday, October 30, 2026: Development I — The Engines and the Store Come Alive
          StatsEngine and EconEngine implemented and validated against your Phase 1 scripts; grouping per routine, staff member and day; the SQLite Store with the tiny-database rule; console reporting. Brick 6 is due Thursday, November 5 (tag alpha-0.2). Bring today's models.py and loader.py: Class 6 builds on them.
